title: Minimum Wage Increases Have a Child Care Problem - The Family Frontier
text:
Minimum Wage Increases Have a Child Care Problem 
 Subscribe Sign in Minimum Wage Increases Have a Child Care Problem
 The chickens of a failed market are roosting right on top of a needed step
 Elliot Haspel Nov 18, 2026 14 1 6 Share Note: Yesterday, Capita released the latest round of our Quarterly Insights from America’s Families survey. Check out the summary write-up, “ The Weight Parents Carry ,” and you can access all of the Quarterly Insights data and track results over time here . 
 The federal minimum wage is $7.25 an hour. It’s been $7.25 an hour since 2009. At $7.25 an hour, you have to work about six hours to afford an average tank of gas, and you have to work almost 14 hours to afford $100 worth of groceries. After Social Security and Medicare are taken out, your yearly take-home pay from working a full-time job — 2,080 hours — is around $14,000.
 The federal minimum wage is too low.
 The Democrats plan to try and do something about that. Per Rachel Cohen Booth ’s reporting in Vox , 
 “I’ve been talking with a lot of different Democrats on the Hill and they’ve been calling it a first 100-day issue,” said Jared Bernstein, who chaired President Joe Biden’s Council of Economic Advisers and is now at the liberal Center for American Progress.
 …A decade after the party rallied around the “Fight for 15” movement, how high to raise the minimum wage — and how fast — is becoming a defining economic question for the new Democratic majority, as well as in states where they have new governing trifectas. In Pennsylvania, Gov. Josh Shapiro has pledged to sign a $15 minimum wage bill , while in Wisconsin, Gov.-elect David Crowley has targeted a gradual increase to $20 . 
 In recent years, a wave of research built on the 30 states that raised their own minimums has convinced many economists that modest increases cost few, if any, jobs. That evidence, plus voters’ anger about the cost of living, has rallied progressive experts around a new federal benchmark equal to two-thirds of the hourly median wage, or roughly $20 by 2030.
 As a good liberal concerned about the well-being of lower-income Americans, this push is welcome. 1 
 However. 
 Lawmakers need to understand — and I want you to understand — that raising the minimum wage has a hidden risk: without a commensurate improvement in public child care funding, minimum wage increases may well further take the knees out from an already buckling child care sector.
 First, let’s level set 
 Child care educators are underpaid. So, so badly underpaid. Absurdly underpaid. Pitifully underpaid. Infuriatingly underpaid. The fact that minimum wage increases can wreak havoc on child care programs — places where literal brains are developed — is a moral stain on the country. 
 Child care educator pay needs to go up. Full stop.
 So let me say this loud and clear up front: any negative impacts of minimum wage increases on child care programs and the families that attend them are not a reason to avoiding raising the minimum wage. They are a reason to increase child care funding as part and parcel of any minimum wage increase . 2 
 It’s worth noting that plenty of child care educators are currently paid more than the minimum wage. The median child care wage is up to a whopping (ugh) $16.82 an hour , although that means half of educators make less and we know there is wide variation by state and region. 3 Still, knowing that starting point means that decisions to raise the minimum wage in a state (or federally) to $15 an hour will, descriptively, impact fewer child care programs than raising it to $20 or $25 an hour. 
 Source That said, one reason that child care wages have been rising in recent years is because programs know they have no choice if they want to maintain enough staff to operate. That in turn is leading programs to raise parent fees to cover the higher wages, which can have the ironic effect of causing under-enrollment because parents aren’t always able to absorb the higher fees — keep that vicious cycle in mind as we move forward. 
 All of this is symptomatic of America’s continued failure to position (and fund with public dollars) child care as a social good that is vital for the health and well-being of children, families, communities, and economies. Early childhood educators shouldn’t be barely clearing poverty wages, but rather offered middle-class salaries with solid benefits. 
 What research says about the minimum wage and child care 
 The reason why minimum wage increases can uniquely harm child care programs, and those who rely on them, is fairly straightforward: most providers have no ability to further raise wages without making damaging choices.
 If you’re McDonalds or a medium-sized manufacturer and the minimum wage raises to $15 an hour but you were previously paying your employees $10 an hour, you are structurally capable of absorbing the increased labor costs — and indeed, as Cohen Booth says, most studies have found few negative impacts on employment , prices, or businesses’ ability to stay open when the minimum wage goes up. The tradeoff seems fairly straightforwardly worth it. 
 However, if you’re a small child care program operating on gossamer-thin margins and you need to increase staff wages from $10 an hour to $15 an hour — as much as you may want to have done so already — then you’re left with only a few choices. You can hike parent fees, reduce staff and the number of kids you can serve, cut benefits (if you have any) or materials or other important budget line items, increase class sizes to the maximum allowable ratio 4 , and/or change who you’re serving to try and bring in a more affluent clientele while enrolling fewer children on state subsidy 5 . None of these are great options! 
 There are a handful of studies looking at what happens to child care specifically when minimum wages go up. They paint a nuanced but not particularly encouraging picture.
 Katharine Sadowski published a 2025 paper for the Census Bureau’s Center for Economic Studies that concluded the way child care programs react to minimum wage increases varies quite a bit by their characteristics and who they are serving — in short, smaller programs and those serving lower-income areas are most likely to respond by closing (and may create openings for chains to grow in their place) while larger programs are most likely to respond to reducing staff. 
 “This study provides the first causal evidence on how minimum wage increases affect the structure of the U.S. childcare industry … While I find no significant effect on the overall number of childcare establishments or workers at the national level, the results point to meaningful heterogeneity in how individual establishments respond. I find establishments in low-income counties are more likely to adjust on the extensive margin, through increased exit, while those in high-income counties tend to adjust on the intensive margin, reducing employment. These patterns are most pronounced among new, smaller, lower-earning, and non-chain firms, while older, larger, and higher-earning firms appear more resilient. In low-income counties. I also find that higher minimum wages are associated with increased entry of larger centers and chains, suggesting a potential shift toward consolidation. While these firms may offer more stability, such changes could alter local availability of care.”
 In 2023, Jessica H. Brown and Chris Herbst published a paper in IZA - Institute of Labor Economics that found most providers deal with the increased costs by raising parent fees, maxing out ratios, or substituting enrollment of families using public subsidy for enrollment of families that can pay full freight. On the plus side, quality goes up as staff levels become more stable and staff have the chance to become better trained. 
 “Although child care firms increase teacher pay in response to minimum wage reforms, we find no impact on employment levels. Instead, providers respond by implementing a range of other revenue-enhancing and cost-saving practices, such as raising prices, increasing child-to-staff ratios, and serving fewer children in the child care subsidy system. 6 We also find evidence that service quality increases: staff turnover declines, teachers are more likely to make human capital investments, and teacher-child interactions improve. Despite the increase in quality, parents report that they are less satisfied with their child care provider, a result we attribute to the increase in prices.” 
 The Washington Center for Equitable Growth summarized the paper’s findings thusly : “As expected from child care’s labor-intensive business model, the higher labor costs resulted in higher prices for families, with center-based market prices increasing between 4.2 percent and 8.1 percent following a 10 percent increase in the minimum wage … In addition to price increases, child care providers adjusted their class sizes and composition to account for increased labor costs. Center-based programs saw enrollment increase by 5.6 percent and child-to-staff ratios rise 4.7 percent. Centers also accepted 12.2 percent fewer subsidized children.” 
 In 2018, a group of researchers at the University of Washington published a peer-reviewed article about the impact of Seattle raising its minimum wage to $15 an hour over the course of the mid-2010s. They concluded : 
 “Providers’ most commonly responded to higher labor costs by raising tuition and reducing staff hours or headcount—strategies that may negatively impact low-income families and staff. While raising wages may help some child care employees, considering the full range of effects of this policy underscores the need for a systems approach to supporting the child care sector as a whole.”
 The researchers also interviewed several Seattle center directors, who offered testimony like “ So I actually started a little emailing several other directors when we were trying to plan what we were going to do … basically asking what they were going to do, right? And so pretty much all of them had like the same uneasy feeling that I did, like, oh, my God, there’s really no way to do this other than to increase tuition. And so that’s why I started calling other places to see if they had any other ideas, and pretty much, no. So everybody’s sort of in the same boat. […] they were all pretty stressed out about it.” and “I just have to [raise tuition] … there’s a cause and effect for doing that. And I’m all for people making more money. But I just have to pass that cost down. And what it does, is it crowds out lower middle class people, which is essentially what I am. And that’s a whole segment of our population that is just … can’t afford housing, can’t afford child care, they make too much to get any subsidies, not enough to get any help, and we’re losing this whole segment of our population.” Another director noted that they had dropped from serving 25 percent children on subsidy to 6 percent, and were no longer attempting to enroll additional subsidy families. 
 A 2026 brief from the Center for the Study of Child Care Employment entitled “ Child Care Centers Compete With California’s $20 Fast Food Wage ” noted that “with the state’s $20 fast food minimum wage, centers are struggling to attract assistants with a $18 to $21 pay range (for voucher-funded programs, only $18 to $20), and the turnover rate for assistants was 29 percent." 
 Again: Does this mean don’t raise the minimum wage? No! 
 Go back to our example of the child care program paying $10 an hour when the minimum wage in their area rises to $15 an hour. If you provide that program with enough public funding to cover a $5 an hour increase, everyone wins: educator wages rise, programs remain solvent and improve in quality, parents don’t have to see a fee increase. I wish I could tell you there was another option, but as the Seattle director said: pretty much, no . 
 I will be cheering on the Democrats in Congress and in governor’s mansions as they attempt to finally raise America’s shamefully low minimum wage. And I will be urging everyone to make sure those lawmakers understand any minimum wage increase needs to be done in direct conjunction with child care funding increases, lest they end up harming both the child care sector and many of the very families they are aiming to help.
 1 And worth talking about now, because if even President Trump blocks these attempts, they’re clearly test runs for 2029.
 2 If you’re wondering: yes, child care centers — and family child care programs that employ outside individuals — are categorically covered by any federal minimum wage increase because of their designation under the Fair Labor Standards Act . 
 3 Not to mention that inflation means that the modest wage increase — median pay was $14.60 back in 2023, for instance — doesn’t actually translate into much increased purchasing power for educators. 
 4 Many programs prefer to operate slightly below the absolute maximum legally allowable capacity in order to allow for staffing flexibility and make it easier to focus on quality.
 5 Which, in most states, reimburses below the true cost of care; so the revenue from a kid on subsidy in that case is less than a kid whose family is full-pay. 
 6 Interestingly, family child care providers (who are largely owner-operated and thus somewhat less exposed to minimum wages in general, although they can be impacted when it comes to the one-third that have at least one hired additional teacher) seem to pick up some of the slack when it comes to those subsidized kids, in that they start enrolling more. However useful that is for the children and families, this ends up being another form of exploitation for a group that is disproportionately made up of older women of color and immigrants: they will take the inadequate reimbursement and sacrifice their own financial security as a result. In fact, when you add up all of the hours they put in, family child care providers often end up with an effective wage below even the current federal minimum wage! All to say, efforts to raise child care wages must, must, must include family child care providers as well.
